clinicalPearls: Consider IPF in an older adult (usually over age 60) with progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough lasting months, especially with a smoking history.
Bibasilar, fine 'Velcro-like' end-inspiratory crackles are the classic auscultatory finding.
Digital clubbing is present in roughly half of patients and supports the diagnosis.

High-resolution CT showing a definite UIP pattern (subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis) can obviate the need for lung biopsy.
IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion — connective tissue disease, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity, and occupational/environmental exposures must be ruled out first.
Course is highly variable: most patients decline gradually, but acute exacerbations with rapid, often fatal deterioration can occur unpredictably.
Antifibrotic therapy slows the rate of decline in lung function but does not reverse existing fibrosis, so early diagnosis and referral matter.
Early referral for lung transplant evaluation should be considered at diagnosis given the poor natural history.
harrison.pathophysiology: IPF is thought to result from repeated micro-injury to alveolar epithelium in a genetically susceptible, typically older individual, triggering an aberrant wound-healing response rather than a primarily inflammatory process. This dysregulated repair leads to fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing the patchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis and architectural distortion characteristic of the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern. Progressive scarring impairs gas exchange and lung compliance, culminating in restrictive physiology and hypoxemia.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT chest — identifies UIP pattern and excludes alternative diagnoses
Pulmonary function tests with DLCO — documents restrictive pattern and gas-transfer impairment, tracks progression
Serologic autoimmune panel (ANA, rheumatoid factor, myositis antibodies) — screens for occult connective tissue disease
Six-minute walk test with oximetry — assesses functional capacity and exertional desaturation
Surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy — considered when HRCT is indeterminate and histopathology would change management
Echocardiogram — evaluates for pulmonary hypertension as a complication
Bronchoalveolar lavage — helps exclude infection or alternative diagnoses in select atypical presentations
Detailed exposure and medication history — identifies occupational, environmental, or drug-related causes of fibrosis
redFlags: Acute worsening of dyspnea over days to weeks (acute exacerbation), which carries high short-term mortality
Resting hypoxemia or significant desaturation on exertion
Rapidly declining forced vital capacity or DLCO on serial testing
Signs of cor pulmonale or pulmonary hypertension
Superimposed respiratory infection, which can precipitate acute decompensation
pitfalls: Attributing crackles and dyspnea to heart failure or COPD without pursuing HRCT, delaying diagnosis
Missing an underlying connective tissue disease or exposure history that would reclassify the disease and change management
Relying on chest x-ray alone, which is insensitive for early fibrotic change
Assuming a stable course; failing to monitor for acute exacerbations or gradual functional decline
harrison.prognosis: IPF carries a poor prognosis with median survival historically around 3-5 years from diagnosis, though the trajectory is heterogeneous and antifibrotic therapy has modestly slowed functional decline. Acute exacerbations and progression to respiratory failure are the major causes of death, and lung transplantation remains the only intervention altering long-term survival.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Interstitial Lung Diseases / Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
management: Start antifibrotic therapy — pirfenidone or nintedanib — to slow the decline in lung function
Provide supplemental oxygen for resting or exertional hypoxaemia and enrol the patient in pulmonary rehabilitation
Manage contributing comorbidities including gastro-oesophageal reflux and pulmonary hypertension, and ensure vaccination against respiratory pathogens
Palliate refractory cough and breathlessness, using opioids for dyspnoea, and integrate palliative care with advance care planning
Treat acute exacerbations supportively after excluding infection and heart failure, recognising corticosteroids are of uncertain benefit
Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests and oximetry and surveil for pulmonary hypertension and lung cancer
Refer suitable candidates early for lung transplantation assessment given the poor prognosis
